title: Automating ITSM with a Healthy CMDB: ServiceNow Best Practices and Workflow Tips
excerpt: Learn how to combine CMDB governance with automation to optimize ServiceNow ITSM workflows. This article covers CMDB best practices, workflow design strategies, and includes two simple code examples for scripted automation.
content:
Overview

ServiceNow ITSM automation delivers the most value when it is built on a healthy, trusted CMDB and well-designed workflows. Without accurate configuration data, automated routing, approvals, and impact analysis quickly become brittle and untrustworthy. This article focuses on practical CMDB best practices and workflow optimization techniques that ServiceNow teams can apply incrementally, with two lightweight code examples to illustrate scripted automation patterns.

CMDB Best Practices for Reliable Automation

A mature CMDB is the backbone of ITSM automation. The goal is not to capture every attribute, but to maintain fit-for-purpose accuracy for the services you are automating.

  • Define clear ownership: Assign service and CI ownership so there is always a accountable person or team for data quality, lifecycle changes, and approvals.
  • Model services first: Start from business services and service offerings, then map supporting applications, servers, and infrastructure. This enables impact-based incident routing, change risk analysis, and SLA alignment.
  • Standardize CI classes and attributes: Restrict the CMDB to a curated set of classes and mandatory attributes that are required by your ITSM processes (incident, change, problem, request).
  • Automate discovery and reconciliation: Use Discovery and IntegrationHub to populate and update CIs, with robust identification rules and reconciliation policies to avoid duplicates and stale records.
  • Govern relationships: Enforce relationship patterns ("Runs on", "Depends on", "Used by") so impact calculation, outage modeling, and change approvals can be automated using dependable topology.
  • Monitor CMDB health: Use CMDB Health KPIs such as completeness, correctness, and compliance, and tie remediation tasks back into ITSM workflows to continuously improve data quality.

Workflow Optimization in ServiceNow ITSM

Once the CMDB is reliable, you can safely automate ITSM workflows across incident, change, and request management.

  • Leverage Flow Designer first: Use Flow Designer and subflows for most automation, reserving Script Actions and Business Rules for edge cases that truly require code.
  • Design modular subflows: Create reusable subflows for patterns like "auto-assign by CI", "notify stakeholders", or "validate CMDB data" to avoid duplicating logic across modules.
  • Use CMDB relationships for routing: Drive incident assignment from the CI’s support group or service owner, and drive change approvals from service and application owners identified in the CMDB.
  • Apply decision tables: For complex routing and approval rules, externalize logic in decision tables so it can be maintained without modifying the flow structure.
  • Build in observability: Log key decisions (priority set, assignment group selected, approver chosen) to help teams understand and trust automated behavior.

Code Example 1: Auto-Assign Incident from CI Support Group

This simple onBefore business rule pattern assigns an incident to the CI’s support group when the user picks a configuration item.

var gr = new GlideRecord('table');
gr.query();

In a real implementation, you would adapt the pattern like this:

if (current.cmdb_ci && !current.assignment_group) {
  var ci = current.cmdb_ci.getRefRecord();
  if (ci.support_group) {
    current.assignment_group = ci.support_group;
  }
}

Code Example 2: Auto-Populate Change Risk from Service Tier

This pattern calculates a simple change risk score based on the business service tier of the affected CI, to be run in a business rule or Script Action.

var affectedCI = current.cmdb_ci;
if (affectedCI) {
  var ci = affectedCI.getRefRecord();
  var service = ci.cmdb_ci_service;
  if (service) {
    var svc = service.getRefRecord();
    switch (svc.tier.toString()) {
      case 'Gold':
        current.risk = '3'; // High
        break;
      case 'Silver':
        current.risk = '2'; // Medium
        break;
      default:
        current.risk = '1'; // Low
    }
  }
}

Conclusion

ServiceNow ITSM automation is only as effective as the CMDB and workflows behind it. By focusing on CMDB governance, service-centric modeling, and modular, observable workflows, you can confidently automate routing, approvals, and risk decisions at scale. Start with a narrow, high-impact process, use Flow Designer wherever possible, and lean on CMDB relationships to keep your automation both powerful and maintainable over time.

title: ServiceNow ITSM Automation: CMDB Best Practices and Workflow Optimization
excerpt: Discover best practices for leveraging ServiceNow's CMDB to enhance ITSM automation and optimize workflows for faster incident resolution and better service delivery. This guide includes practical code examples to implement these strategies effectively.
content:
Introduction to ITSM Automation in ServiceNow

ServiceNow's IT Service Management (ITSM) platform excels in automation, particularly through its Configuration Management Database (CMDB) and advanced workflow tools. By applying ITIL-aligned best practices, organizations can centralize IT asset relationships, streamline change processes, and automate incident routing for operational excellence.

CMDB Best Practices for ITSM Automation

The CMDB serves as a central repository for IT assets and their relationships, enabling impact analysis during incidents and changes. Keeping CMDB records accurate and current improves decision-making and visibility into the IT environment.

  • Maintain Data Accuracy: Regularly audit and update CMDB entries to reflect real-world configurations, reducing errors in incident and change management.
  • Leverage Relationships: Map dependencies between configuration items (CIs) to automate impact assessments and prioritize issues based on business criticality.
  • Integrate with Discovery Tools: Use ServiceNow Discovery to populate and synchronize CMDB automatically, minimizing manual data entry.
  • Implement Governance: Establish roles for CMDB stewardship to ensure compliance with ITIL standards and continuous improvement.

These practices align with ITIL principles, standardizing ITSM processes for consistent service delivery.

Workflow Optimization Strategies

ServiceNow's Flow Designer enables low-code automation, replacing legacy workflows with modular, maintainable flows. Key best practices include using subflows for reusability, decision tables for complex routing, and robust error handling to prevent disruptions.

  • Adopt Modular Design: Build subflows that accept record references as inputs, accessing fields dynamically to adapt to changes without breaking workflows.
  • Automate Incident Routing: Use AI-driven categorization, priority setting, and assignment based on CI relationships for faster resolution.
  • Incorporate Error Handlers: Capture diagnostics, notify admins, and log audits to ensure graceful failures.
  • Test Incrementally: Simulate executions in Flow Designer to validate success and error paths before production deployment.

Optimizing workflows reduces manual intervention, enhances SLA adherence, and boosts customer satisfaction.

Code Example 1: Querying CMDB for Incident Impact Analysis

This script queries related CIs in the CMDB to assess incident impact, a core automation for problem management.

var incidentSysId = current.sys_id; // From incident record

var gr = new GlideRecord('cmdb_ci');
gr.addQuery('affected_by', incidentSysId);
gr.query();

while (gr.next()) {
    gs.info('Affected CI: ' + gr.name + ' (Impact: High)');
    // Trigger notifications or escalations
}

Code Example 2: Automated Workflow Approval Using Flow Designer Script

In a Flow Designer subflow, use this script step for dynamic approval routing based on request cost and department.

var request = fd.data.request_record; // Data pill from input
var cost = request.cost;
var dept = request.department;

if (cost > 10000 || dept == 'Finance') {
    fd.data.approver = 'sys_id_of_vp'; // Set data pill for VP approval
} else {
    fd.data.approver = 'sys_id_of_manager';
}

Implementing for Success

Start with process assessments to identify bottlenecks, then build incrementally. Integrate AI for predictive routing and leverage ITIL for governance. These steps ensure scalable ITSM automation that evolves with business needs.

By focusing on CMDB accuracy and workflow modularity, your organization can achieve faster resolutions and superior service quality.

title: Inside the Latest ServiceNow AI Platform Updates: Release Notes, Security, and Performance
excerpt: A concise tour of the latest ServiceNow AI Platform (Zurich and late Yokohama) updates with a focus on release notes, security hardening, and performance improvements. Includes practical code snippets to help admins and developers quickly validate, secure, and tune their instances.
content:
Overview

The latest ServiceNow AI Platform releases, including Yokohama and Zurich, continue the platform’s emphasis on secure-by-default configurations, AI-assisted operations, and performance observability. For technical writers, admins, and developers, this cycle of updates brings richer release documentation, targeted security patches, and several performance-focused capabilities that translate directly into clearer upgrade guidance and safer change planning.

From an authoring perspective, the key themes are tighter governance over core platform behavior, better diagnostics for slow experiences, and incremental hardening of integrations and data access. These changes are designed to minimize risk during upgrades while still enabling teams to adopt new capabilities quickly.

Release Notes Highlights

ServiceNow now packages its AI Platform release information with clearer family-level and product-specific notes, making it easier to trace individual fixes back to a specific component. Zurich continues this pattern with structured release notes for core features, UI, and domain applications, helping teams differentiate between breaking changes, deprecated features, and low-risk enhancements.

On the platform side, Zurich introduces richer analytics through User Experience Analytics, giving administrators a built-in way to track load times, event hot spots, and page popularity. These data points, combined with enhanced scheduling options in Scheduled Jobs and Flow triggers, allow more precise timing of heavy workloads so they avoid peak usage windows and support upgrade playbooks with concrete before-and-after metrics.

Developer tooling release notes also call out updates like enhanced Workflow Studio and Catalog Builder client scripting. These help content owners document more prescriptive development standards, especially around how to build reliable automations and catalog items that remain compatible across family upgrades.

Security Patch and Hardening Updates

Recent family releases continue ServiceNow’s pattern of silent security hardening: default roles are tightened, legacy interfaces are retired, and new guardrails are added around integrations and clone behavior. In Zurich, the Clone Admin Console gains finer control over preserving in-progress work, which indirectly supports safer adoption of security patches by reducing the risk of lost configuration work when preparing test clones.

Security operations products also benefit from AI enhancements that surface likely root causes faster, reducing the exposure window between detection and containment. While many of these fixes arrive as part of standard patch levels rather than headline features, they are supported by clearer documentation of changed properties, new sys_properties defaults, and explicit notes about deprecated endpoints.

From a documentation and governance standpoint, this means you can capture a more precise view of what each patch level changes, and describe the expected impact on access controls, data protection behaviors, and integration credentials.

Code example: checking for security-patched records

Use a simple GlideRecord check in a non‑prod clone to confirm that specific security updates are present before promoting content:

var gr = new GlideRecord('sys_update_xml');
gr.addQuery('name', 'CONTAINS', 'Security Fix');
gr.query();
while (gr.next()) {
  gs.info('Security update applied: ' + gr.name);
}

Performance and Reliability Fixes

Performance remains a central theme in the latest releases. Zurich’s User Experience Analytics and enhancements to Service Portal (such as deferred widget loading) provide native instrumentation that once required custom logging or third-party tools. Admins can now correlate page-level performance with specific widgets, client scripts, and scheduled workloads more easily.

New scheduling patterns for Scheduled Jobs and Flow triggers allow teams to move heavy operations—such as nightly reconciliation, large data loads, and report generation—into narrow windows that reduce impact on end-users. For technical writers, these features are important to document as recommended patterns in runbooks and platform operations guides.

Code example: spotting slow-running transactions

For targeted troubleshooting, you can query the transaction log (where accessible) and flag long-running requests in a performance test clone:

var gr = new GlideRecord('syslog_transaction');
gr.addQuery('response_time', '>', 2000);
gr.orderByDesc('response_time');
gr.setLimit(20);
gr.query();
while (gr.next()) {
  gs.info(gr.url + ' took ' + gr.response_time + ' ms');
}

Code example: deferring heavy background work

To align with the newer scheduling guidance, wrap expensive tasks in Scheduled Script Executions that run during low-traffic periods:

var gr = new GlideRecord('cmdb_ci');
gr.query();
while (gr.next()) {
  // Lightweight operation or batched updates
  gr.setValue('u_last_maintenance_check', new GlideDateTime());
  gr.update();
}

Conclusion

The current generation of ServiceNow AI Platform releases blends incremental hardening, richer diagnostics, and operational flexibility rather than introducing disruptive platform changes. By closely following the structured release notes for Zurich and late Yokohama, teams can document exactly how security patches and performance fixes affect their environments, support safer upgrades, and embed these new capabilities into their development and operations standards.

title: ServiceNow ITSM Automation: CMDB, Workflow Optimization, and Hyperautomation
excerpt: Practical patterns and implementation guidance for designing a reliable CMDB, optimizing ITSM workflows with Flow Designer, and building toward hyperautomation on ServiceNow. Focused on incident/change/problem/request use cases, decision logic, and governance so dev teams can implement safely at scale.
content:
Overview

This guide focuses on three areas for ServiceNow ITSM teams:

  • CMDB best practices to make automation reliable.
  • Workflow optimization using Flow Designer and ITIL-aligned processes.
  • Hyperautomation patterns that combine CMDB, ITSM, ITOM, and AI.

It is written for ServiceNow developers and platform owners who want concrete implementation guidance rather than theory.

1. CMDB Best Practices for Automation

Your automation is only as good as your CMDB. Treat the CMDB as a product with clear ownership, standards, and quality controls.

1.1 CMDB design principles

  • Model services, not just servers
    Implement a top-down model: Business Service → Application Service → Infrastructure CIs. Use Service Offerings and relationships (Runs on, Depends on, Hosted on) to support incident and change impact analysis.
  • Standardize CI classes and attributes
    Define a minimal, mandatory attribute set per CI class (e.g., owner, environment, criticality, support group). Avoid bloated schemas that no one maintains.
  • Use relationships aggressively
    Automations such as auto-assignment, impact analysis, and change approvals can key off relationships like Depends on, Used by, and Owned by.
  • Separate discovery source from truth
    Use multiple data sources (Discovery, SCCM/Intune, cloud APIs) but normalize into a single canonical CI per asset. Maintain data source precedence rules.

1.2 CMDB data quality and governance

  • Define CMDB SLOs
    Examples: CI completeness ≥ 95% for critical services, relationship accuracy ≥ 90% for production business services. Track via reports and dashboards.
  • Automated data quality checks
    Schedule jobs or flows that detect anomalies (orphaned CIs, missing owners, CIs without relationships, duplicates) and open tasks for CI owners.
  • Ownership model
    Assign Service owners (business and technical) per business service, and CI owners for key infrastructure classes. Use these for approvals, notifications, and escalation.
  • Change-driven CMDB updates
    Enforce that changes to production infrastructure/services must update the CMDB as part of the change workflow (tasks or automated discovery re-scans post-implementation).

1.3 CMDB patterns that enable specific automations

  • Incident auto-assignment
    Pattern: Incident → CI → Assignment group / Support group on CI.
    Implementation: a Flow Designer flow on Incident insert/update that resolves the CI, then chooses assignment group based on CI.support_group or service owner.
  • Change impact analysis
    Pattern: Change → CI(s) → Related services → Dependent incidents/requests.
    Implementation: script action or flow that walks relationships from affected CIs to Business Services, then attaches impacted CIs/services and notifies owners.
  • Risk scoring
    Pattern: Risk = f(CI criticality, environment, service tier, change type, historical failures).
    Implementation: Decision table that uses CI attributes to assign risk; use in Change workflows for CAB vs. standard changes.

2. Workflow Optimization (Flow Designer First)

Modern ITSM automation should be implemented primarily with Flow Designer and subflows, keeping scripts small and well-encapsulated.

2.1 General workflow design best practices

  • Flow Designer as default
    Use Flow Designer for incident, request, change, and problem flows. Reserve server/client scripts for logic that is not expressible in standard actions or where performance is critical.
  • Modular subflows
    Create reusable subflows for common actions such as notifications, approvals, assignment lookups, and SLA calculations. This promotes consistency and easier maintenance across ITSM processes.

3. Hyperautomation Patterns: CMDB + ITSM + ITOM + AI

Hyperautomation extends traditional workflow automation by combining multiple ServiceNow capabilities into intelligent, self-healing systems.

3.1 Event-driven incident creation (ITOM → ITSM)

  • Pattern: Alert → Event Rule → Incident with CI auto-populated
  • Implementation: Configure Event Management to correlate alerts, deduplicate, and auto-create incidents. Use alert rules to map alerts to CIs via CMDB relationships, ensuring incidents have correct assignment groups from day one.

3.2 Predictive Intelligence for ticket routing

  • Pattern: New Incident → ML model → Auto-assignment + category prediction
  • Implementation: Train Predictive Intelligence models on historical incident data. Enable auto-population of Category, Assignment Group, and Priority based on short description analysis. Combine with CMDB lookups for validation.

3.3 Virtual Agent + Flow Designer for self-service resolution

  • Pattern: User query → Virtual Agent → Flow Designer → Auto-resolution or ticket creation
  • Implementation: Build Virtual Agent topics that invoke Flow Designer subflows for common requests (password resets, access requests, status checks). Use CMDB to validate user entitlements and CI ownership.

3.4 Closed-loop remediation (AIOps)

  • Pattern: Alert → Incident → Automated remediation → Verification → Auto-close
  • Implementation: For known error patterns, trigger remediation flows (restart service, clear cache, scale resources) via Integration Hub or MID Server commands. Verify resolution via health checks before auto-closing the incident.

3.5 Governance and guardrails

  • Start with high-confidence, low-risk automations (notifications, routing) before enabling auto-remediation.
  • Implement approval gates for destructive actions.
  • Log all automated decisions for audit and model retraining.
  • Set thresholds: only auto-resolve when ML confidence exceeds 90%.

Conclusion

Effective ITSM automation on ServiceNow requires a solid CMDB foundation, modular Flow Designer workflows, and a phased approach to hyperautomation. Start with reliable data, build reusable components, and progressively enable AI-driven capabilities with appropriate governance.

title: ServiceNow Developer Core APIs & Platform Fundamentals (Zurich/Yokohama Era)
excerpt: Practical reference to current ServiceNow server-side and integration APIs with a focus on core primitives, Flow Designer internals, performance, and security fundamentals for scoped app developers.
content:
Overview

This reference distills current ServiceNow platform fundamentals for developers building scalable, upgrade-safe applications and integrations. It focuses on the Glide server APIs, integration primitives, Flow Designer behavior, performance patterns, and security concepts that remain stable across recent releases (Zurich/Yokohama generation).

Core Server-Side APIs

GlideRecord

Purpose: Synchronous CRUD and querying on tables; primary server-side data API.

Core usage pattern

// Query incidents with state=2 (In Progress) and short_description contains keyword
var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr.addQuery('state', 2);
gr.addQuery('short_description', 'CONTAINS', 'network');
gr.query();
while (gr.next()) {
  gs.info('Incident: ' + gr.number + ' - ' + gr.short_description);
}

GlideAggregate

Purpose: Efficient COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX operations without loading full records.

// Count active incidents by priority
var ga = new GlideAggregate('incident');
ga.addQuery('active', true);
ga.addAggregate('COUNT');
ga.groupBy('priority');
ga.query();
while (ga.next()) {
  gs.info('Priority ' + ga.priority + ': ' + ga.getAggregate('COUNT'));
}

GlideRecord Best Practices

  • Use GlideAggregate for counts and sums instead of looping through GlideRecord results.
  • Always add appropriate query filters to limit result sets.
  • Use setLimit() when you only need a subset of records.
  • Avoid dot-walking in loops; cache reference values before iteration.

Integration APIs

RESTMessageV2

Purpose: Outbound REST calls to external systems with authentication, headers, and payload management.

// Outbound REST call with OAuth 2.0
var rm = new sn_ws.RESTMessageV2('My_REST_Message', 'POST');
rm.setStringParameterNoEscape('endpoint', 'https://api.example.com/data');
rm.setRequestHeader('Content-Type', 'application/json');
rm.setRequestBody(JSON.stringify({ key: 'value' }));

var response = rm.execute();
var httpStatus = response.getStatusCode();
var body = response.getBody();

if (httpStatus == 200) {
  var parsed = JSON.parse(body);
  gs.info('Response: ' + parsed.result);
} else {
  gs.error('REST call failed: ' + httpStatus);
}

Scripted REST APIs

Purpose: Expose custom inbound REST endpoints for external systems to call ServiceNow.

// Scripted REST Resource (GET method)
(function process(request, response) {
  var incidentId = request.pathParams.id;
  var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
  
  if (gr.get(incidentId)) {
    response.setStatus(200);
    response.setBody({
      number: gr.number.toString(),
      short_description: gr.short_description.toString(),
      state: gr.state.getDisplayValue()
    });
  } else {
    response.setStatus(404);
    response.setBody({ error: 'Incident not found' });
  }
})(request, response);

Flow Designer Internals

Execution Context

Flow Designer flows execute in a dedicated context with access to trigger data, input variables, and step outputs. Understanding execution boundaries is critical for debugging.

  • Trigger context: Contains the record or event that initiated the flow.
  • Step outputs: Each action step produces outputs accessible to subsequent steps via data pills.
  • Transaction boundaries: By default, flows run in a single transaction; use async subflows to break transaction scope.

Error Handling Patterns

// Script step with try-catch for external calls
(function execute(inputs, outputs) {
  try {
    var rm = new sn_ws.RESTMessageV2('External_API', 'GET');
    var response = rm.execute();
    
    if (response.getStatusCode() != 200) {
      outputs.success = false;
      outputs.error_message = 'API returned ' + response.getStatusCode();
      return;
    }
    
    outputs.success = true;
    outputs.data = JSON.parse(response.getBody());
  } catch (e) {
    outputs.success = false;
    outputs.error_message = e.message;
  }
})(inputs, outputs);

Subflow Reuse

Extract common logic into subflows for reusability. Subflows can be called from multiple parent flows and accept input/output variables.

  • Use subflows for: notifications, approvals, assignment logic, external API calls.
  • Keep subflows focused on a single responsibility.
  • Version subflows carefully—changes affect all calling flows.

Performance Patterns

Query Optimization

  • Use indexes: Query on indexed fields (sys_id, number, active, state) for fast lookups.
  • Avoid wildcard starts: CONTAINS and STARTSWITH are efficient; avoid patterns like ENDSWITH which cannot use indexes.
  • Limit results: Always use setLimit() when you need only a subset of records.
// Efficient: Query on indexed field with limit
var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr.addQuery('active', true);
gr.addQuery('priority', 1);
gr.orderByDesc('sys_created_on');
gr.setLimit(50);
gr.query();

Async Processing

Move heavy operations to background processing to avoid blocking user transactions.

// Schedule heavy work asynchronously
var worker = new GlideScriptedHierarchicalWorker();
worker.setProgressName('Bulk CI Update');
worker.setScriptIncludeName('BulkCIProcessor');
worker.setScriptIncludeMethod('process');
worker.putMethodArg('batchSize', 500);
worker.setBackground(true);
worker.start();

Caching Strategies

  • Use GlideSystem cache for frequently accessed configuration data.
  • Cache reference field values before loops to avoid repeated database calls.
  • Leverage system properties (gs.getProperty()) which are automatically cached.

Security Fundamentals

ACL Evaluation Order

ServiceNow evaluates ACLs in a specific order. Understanding this prevents security gaps.

  1. Table-level ACLs (e.g., incident.*)
  2. Field-level ACLs (e.g., incident.work_notes)
  3. Row-level conditions within ACLs

ACLs are AND-ed together: a user must pass ALL applicable ACLs to access a record or field.

Scoped Application Security

  • Application scope: Isolates custom tables, scripts, and configurations from global scope.
  • Cross-scope access: Requires explicit access grants via Application Cross-Scope Access records.
  • Script Include access: Mark Script Includes as Client Callable only when necessary; prefer server-side calls.
// Check user role before sensitive operation
if (!gs.hasRole('admin') && !gs.hasRole('itil')) {
  gs.addErrorMessage('Insufficient privileges for this operation');
  current.setAbortAction(true);
  return;
}

API Access Controls

  • Scripted REST APIs inherit table ACLs by default; add explicit role requirements for sensitive endpoints.
  • Use OAuth 2.0 or token-based auth for external integrations instead of basic auth.
  • Audit API access via Transaction Logs and API Usage Analytics.

Common Anti-Patterns

  • Querying without filters: Never call gr.query() without adding conditions on large tables.
  • Dot-walking in loops: Cache reference values before iteration to avoid N+1 query problems.
  • Synchronous external calls in Business Rules: Move external API calls to async flows or scheduled jobs.
  • Hardcoding sys_ids: Use system properties or reference fields instead of hardcoded identifiers.
  • Ignoring transaction limits: Be aware of the 10,000 record and 300-second transaction limits in synchronous operations.

Conclusion

Mastering these core APIs, Flow Designer patterns, performance techniques, and security fundamentals provides the foundation for building enterprise-grade ServiceNow applications. Focus on indexed queries, async processing for heavy workloads, proper ACL design, and modular flow architecture to ensure your solutions scale reliably across Zurich, Yokohama, and future releases.

title: This Week in ServiceNow: December 2025 Platform & Store Updates for Architects and Developers
excerpt: A curated, implementation-focused view of this week’s ServiceNow platform, Store, and Employee Center updates. Learn what matters for architecture, upgrades, extensibility, and enterprise risk so you can make informed design and implementation decisions.
content:
Overview

This week’s ServiceNow updates focus on three big themes: AI-first platform capabilities, platform health & observability, and experience-layer enhancements for employees and knowledge workers. Architects, Implementers, and Developers should treat these as inputs into 2026 roadmap planning, upgrade strategy, and governance models.

Highlights include:

  • New Yokohama family patches and hotfixes introducing AI, automation, and governance refinements.
  • New Knowledge Center workspace with advanced editing and AI-assisted knowledge workflows.
  • Employee Center (Pro) December 2025 enhancements focused on engagement, targeting, and extensibility.
  • Impact Platform Health and Store updates that deepen diagnostics, real-time prevention, and observability.
  • Security, performance, and upgrade guidance that directly affect enterprise-scale implementations.

Latest Release Updates & Architectural Impact

Yokohama patches & hotfixes

The Yokohama family now lists updated patches and hotfixes, including security and performance fixes that are individually shippable and can be applied without a major family upgrade.

  • Architectural impact: Yokohama continues to expand AI capabilities (AI Governance, Now Assist, AI Search) and industry solutions. These features assume a more mature data model, tighter RBAC, and AI usage governance.
  • Upgrade strategy: Move away from "big bang" family jumps toward smaller, more frequent patch adoption. This aligns with ServiceNow’s guidance to "upgrade with app version" for more granular control of app-level changes.
  • Implementation risk: AI features touch knowledge, search, and case workflows. Misaligned ACLs, knowledge governance, or inconsistent taxonomies can cause incorrect AI responses or overexposure of content.

Sample upgrade readiness script to quickly surface customizations against a critical table before adopting a patch:

// List customizations on a key table before patching
(function() {
  var TABLE = 'incident';
  var gr = new GlideRecord('sys_metadata');
  gr.addQuery('name', TABLE);
  gr.addQuery('sys_scope.scope', '!=', 'global');
  gr.query();
  gs.info('Customizations on ' + TABLE + ':');
  while (gr.next()) {
    gs.info(gr.getDisplayValue('sys_class_name') + ' - ' + gr.getDisplayValue('sys_scope'));
  }
})();

AI Governance & AI Search (Yokohama)

Yokohama introduces AI Governance with a unified AI asset inventory and governance workflows, plus improved Now Assist AI Search for Genius Results and deflection.

  • Define an enterprise-wide AI data contract (which tables, fields, and attachments are AI-eligible) and enforce via dictionary attributes and ACLs.
  • Centralize configuration in a dedicated AI Platform or Center of Excellence application for repeatability.
// Example: flag a field as AI-excludable via dictionary attribute
var dict = new GlideRecord('sys_dictionary');
if (dict.get('incident.short_description')) {
  dict.attributes = (dict.attributes || '') + ',ai_exclude=true';
  dict.update();
}

Platform Health, Impact & Observability

New Impact Platform Health capabilities

The December 2025 Store release for Impact Platform Health brings real-time messaging & prevention, scheduled diagnostic scans, and dashboards.

  • Scalability: Automated scans detect patterns (e.g., unindexed queries, inefficient scripts, high-risk integrations) before they impact performance.
  • Governance: Findings can be routed into governed remediation workflows and linked to Architecture Review Boards.

Example: create an on-demand diagnostic scan trigger script for admins:

// Trigger a Platform Health scan for a specific scope
(function() {
  var scopeName = 'x_acme_finance';
  var ph = new sn_impact.platform_health.ScanRequest();
  ph.setScope(scopeName);
  ph.setPriority('high');
  ph.execute();
})();

Anti-pattern: Treating Platform Health as a one-time go-live step. Instead, schedule scans nightly/weekly and review findings as a recurring SRE/architecture ceremony.

Employee Center & Store Updates

Employee Center (Pro) – December 2025 enhancements

The December 2025 Employee Center Pro update introduces improvements focused on content targeting, extensibility, and integration with HRSD Store features.

  • Adoption guidance:
    • Standardize on Employee Center as the single front door; phase out custom portals by mapping key journeys (IT, HR, Facilities, Procurement) into unified experiences.
    • Use topic pages, campaigns, and audience targeting to reduce navigation complexity.
  • Extensibility:
    • Package custom widgets and pages into custom scopes for easier Store-aligned upgrades.
    • Use configuration records (menus, cards, content) instead of hard-coded UI Scripts.
// Simple example: dynamically set Employee Center audience tag
var ecAudience = new GlideRecord('sn_ec_audience');
ecAudience.initialize();
ecAudience.name = 'Managers - North America';
ecAudience.active = true;
ecAudience.condition = 'user.country=Canada^ORuser.country=United States^user.rolesLIKEmanager';
ecAudience.insert();

Anti-pattern: Copying Service Portal widgets and directly embedding them into Employee Center. Use the supported Employee Center framework and configuration points to avoid brittle dependencies.

HR Service Delivery Store – December 2025

The HRSD December 2025 Store deep dive highlights enhancements that often surface through Employee Center (Pro): improved case experiences, AI-assisted HR interactions, and better content experiences.

  • Ensure HR, IT, and Corporate Comms share a common information architecture for knowledge, services, and campaigns.
  • Use Store versions to decouple HRSD innovation from core platform family upgrades.

Knowledge Center & Content Lifecycle

New Knowledge Center workspace

ServiceNow introduced Knowledge Center, a new workspace designed to simplify the entire knowledge lifecycle with advanced editing and AI assistance.

  • Architectural implications:
    • Knowledge becomes a first-class, governed asset with lifecycle states, ownership, and quality controls.
    • AI experiences (search, deflection, agents) depend heavily on this curated knowledge base.
  • Implementation guidance:
    • Standardize article templates by domain (IT, HR, Security, Facilities) to improve AI quality.
    • Use Knowledge Center’s workflows for review, translation, and retirement instead of custom flows.
// Example: Enforce mandatory template for IT knowledge articles
(function() {
  var k = new GlideRecord('kb_knowledge');
  k.addQuery('kb_knowledge_base', 'IT_KB_SYS_ID');
  k.addQuery('u_template_used', false);
  k.setLimit(100);
  k.query();
  while (k.next()) {
    gs.warn('Article without template: ' + k.number);
  }
})();

Anti-pattern: Allowing free-form, unstructured articles. This dramatically reduces the value of AI search and Now Assist and increases maintenance costs.

Security, Vulnerability Fixes & Performance

Patches and security posture

Yokohama patches and hotfixes frequently include security and performance fixes. For regulated industries and public sector, timely adoption is an architectural requirement, not just operational hygiene.

  • Integrate patch evaluation into your Change Advisory Board with a standard checklist: assets affected, scopes impacted, regression test coverage.
  • Use Automated Test Framework (ATF) suites to validate after patching core apps (Incident, HR, CSM, GRC).
// Minimal smoke ATF test for catalog submission
var test = new sn_atf.AutomatedTesting();
var suiteId = test.createTestSuite('Post-Patch Smoke Suite');
var testId = test.createTest('Submit standard item', suiteId);
// Add steps via API or UI; here we just log the suite
gs.info('Created ATF suite: ' + suiteId);

Anti-pattern: Skipping ATF and relying only on manual, ad-hoc regression testing after security patches.

Actionable Best Practices & Design Patterns

  • Treat AI as a platform capability, not an app: Govern AI asset inventory, data contracts, and risk assessments centrally.
  • Adopt Platform Health as SRE tooling: Run scheduled scans, track findings as backlog items, and measure mean time to remediation for platform issues.
  • Standardize on Employee Center as the UX front door: Rationalize legacy portals and unify service catalogs and knowledge across domains.
  • Use Store app versioning deliberately: Align HRSD and other Store app upgrades with business release trains while keeping platform patches flowing.
  • Codify governance with scripts & policies: Use GlideRecord utilities, ATF, and configuration policies to enforce consistency (naming, scoping, templates, ACLs).

Common Pitfalls

  • Enabling AI features without hardening knowledge, RBAC, and data residency controls first.
  • Treating Platform Health and Impact as optional add-ons instead of core observability tooling.
  • Over-customizing Employee Center with cloned widgets and unsupported client scripts.
  • Deferring Yokohama patches because "nothing is broken" and then accumulating security debt.
  • Allowing every team to define its own article structures, taxonomies, and deflection logic.

title: Building on ServiceNow’s Latest AI: Now Assist, AI Control Tower, and Agentic Patterns for Developers
excerpt: Explore the newest ServiceNow AI capabilities—from Now Assist model v2.0 and AI Control Tower to Virtual Agent, AI Search, and agent-to-agent patterns. Learn concrete implementation techniques using GlideRecord and Flow Designer so you can safely plug GenAI and LLMs into real workflows.
content:
Overview

ServiceNow continues to expand its AI Platform with deeper GenAI, safer orchestration, and richer virtual agent capabilities. Recent releases introduce upgraded Now Assist models, enhanced governance with AI Control Tower, and new agentic automation patterns that span workflows and external LLMs.

For developers, the value is twofold: you can now embed powerful AI into everyday flows (summaries, routing, answers) while keeping strict control over data, models, and observability. This article focuses on practical implementation patterns using GlideRecord, Flow Designer, and out-of-box AI components.

Now Assist and GenAI Updates

ServiceNow’s new AI models and Now Assist experiences deliver better summarization, answer quality, and workspace integration across ITSM, CSM, HR, and Employee Center.

Key capabilities

  • Now Assist models v2.0 with improved intent understanding, summarization, and adherence to platform security boundaries.
  • Embedded GenAI in workspaces for incident, case, and knowledge summarization, draft responses, and content generation.
  • Knowledge Center with AI-assisted editing for faster article creation and refinement.

Actionable implementation pattern: AI-driven incident summary

Typical flow:

  1. Agent opens an incident in Workspace.
  2. Now Assist generates a summary from activity and related records.
  3. Agent optionally stores the summary back on the record.

To persist a GenAI-generated summary using GlideRecord in a Script Action or Script Include:

// Called from a UI Action or Flow Designer Action when the agent accepts a Now Assist summary
(function(storeSummary) {
  if (!storeSummary.incident_sys_id || !storeSummary.summary_text)
    return;

  var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
  if (gr.get(storeSummary.incident_sys_id)) {
    gr.u_ai_summary = storeSummary.summary_text; // Custom field to store AI output
    gr.update();
  }
})({
  incident_sys_id: current.sys_id,
  summary_text: inputs.summary // Passed from Flow or UI
});

Best practice: persist only necessary AI outputs (e.g., summary, classification) and avoid storing raw prompts or sensitive content.

AI Control Tower and Predictive Intelligence

AI Control Tower centralizes model selection, governance, and observability for Now Assist, Predictive Intelligence, and integrated LLMs. Predictive Intelligence continues to power auto-routing, auto-classification, and recommendations.

Control Tower patterns

  • Define per-use-case policies (e.g., which LLM for summarization vs. classification).
  • Enable logging and guardrails for prompts and responses (mask PII where required).
  • Route traffic between Now LLM and partner models (e.g., Microsoft, OpenAI) while retaining platform security controls.

Predictive Intelligence auto-routing in Flow Designer

Example: Classify and route new incidents using a trained model, then fall back to business rules if confidence is low.

// Script step in Flow Designer: Evaluate PI classification confidence
var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
if (!gr.get(current.sys_id)) {
  outputs.is_confident = false;
  return;
}

// Assume a classification result is stored by an OOB PI action
var confidence = parseFloat(gr.u_pi_confidence || 0);
outputs.is_confident = confidence >= 0.8;

Then use a Flow Designer Decision:

  • If is_confident == true → set assignment group from PI prediction.
  • Else → route to default triage queue.

Virtual Agent AI and NLU Updates

Virtual Agent leverages updated NLU and GenAI to handle more complex dialogs, summarize conversations, and draft resolutions.

Patterns to implement

  • Use topic triggers that rely on new NLU models for broader intent coverage.
  • Call Now Assist within a Virtual Agent topic to summarize the chat and store it on the associated record.
  • Attach GenAI-generated resolution text to incident or case work notes from within the topic.

Example: Virtual Agent topic script to persist a GenAI chat summary:

// In a VA Script step (Client callable Script Include pattern)
var VaAiUtils = Class.create();
VaAiUtils.prototype = {
  initialize: function() {},

  saveSummaryToIncident: function(incidentId, summary) {
    if (!incidentId || !summary)
      return false;

    var inc = new GlideRecord('incident');
    if (!inc.get(incidentId))
      return false;

    inc.work_notes = 'AI chat summary:\n' + summary;
    inc.update();
    return true;
  },

  type: 'VaAiUtils'
};

Agent-to-Agent (A2A), MCP, and LLM Integration

ServiceNow’s agentic vision includes AI agents that collaborate with human agents and external systems. Through AI Control Tower and partner integrations (e.g., Microsoft), you can orchestrate multi-agent workflows while keeping governance centralized.

Agent-to-Agent & MCP patterns

  • Use Flow Designer to orchestrate calls between Now Assist, external LLMs, and internal APIs.
  • Configure AI Control Tower policies to direct which agent or LLM owns each task (classification, summarization, content generation).
  • Integrate with Microsoft collaboration surfaces so AI agents can coordinate resolutions from Teams while updating ServiceNow records.

Example: Flow Designer orchestrated multi-agent flow

  1. Trigger: Incident created.
  2. Action 1: Now Assist summarizes description and context.
  3. Action 2: Predictive Intelligence suggests assignment group.
  4. Action 3: External LLM via HTTP step drafts a customer-facing update.
  5. Action 4: GlideRecord step stores outputs and posts a work note.
// Example Script step in Flow Designer combining AI outputs
(function execute(inputs, outputs) {
  var inc = new GlideRecord('incident');
  if (!inc.get(current.sys_id))
    return;

  // Inputs from previous AI actions
  var aiSummary = inputs.ai_summary || '';
  var aiReply   = inputs.ai_reply || '';

  if (aiSummary)
    inc.u_ai_summary = aiSummary;

  if (aiReply)
    inc.comments = 'Suggested reply (AI):\n' + aiReply;

  inc.update();
})(inputs, outputs);

LLM Integration Patterns and AI Search

ServiceNow supports flexible LLM choices through AI Control Tower, plus AI Search to provide semantic, relevance-ranked results across knowledge and records.

Recommended patterns

  • Use AI Search as the primary entry point for AI-powered Q&A instead of calling LLMs directly for data retrieval.
  • Combine AI Search results + Now Assist to generate grounded answers that reference specific articles or records.
  • Configure index sources carefully (knowledge, catalog, cases) to avoid exposing sensitive data.

Example: Scripted AI Search query + answer generation pattern

// Pseudo-pattern: use AI Search for grounding, then pass snippets to GenAI
var query = 'reset VPN password';
var searchGr = new GlideRecord('sa_ai_search_result');
searchGr.addQuery('query_string', query);
searchGr.query();

var snippets = [];
while (searchGr.next() && snippets.length < 3) {
  snippets.push(searchGr.getValue('snippet')); // Hypothetical field
}

// Concatenate snippets and send to a Now Assist or LLM action via Flow
outputs.context_snippets = snippets.join('\n---\n');

Best Practices

  • Start with high-value, low-risk use cases like summaries, routing, and draft responses before moving to autonomous actions.
  • Use AI Control Tower for every production GenAI use case to manage providers, guardrails, and observability.
  • Keep prompts and outputs minimal and avoid sending unnecessary fields or PII to external models.
  • Ground GenAI with AI Search and concrete record data to improve accuracy and reduce hallucinations.
  • Capture metrics (accept/override, resolution time, CSAT) to continuously tune Predictive Intelligence and Now Assist configurations.
  • Use Script Includes as thin AI facades so flows, UI Actions, and Virtual Agent topics share the same logic.

Common Pitfalls

  • Calling LLMs directly for system-of-record queries instead of using AI Search or GlideRecord, leading to inaccurate or stale answers.
  • Bypassing AI Control Tower and hardcoding provider endpoints, which breaks governance, observability, and future portability.
  • Overloading prompts with entire records (including sensitive fields) rather than narrowing to relevant attributes.
  • Letting AI auto-update records without human review for high-risk actions like approvals, major incident communication, or HR decisions.
  • Ignoring model versioning when moving to newer Now Assist models, resulting in untested behavior changes in production workflows.
  • Embedding complex business logic inside prompts (“do X except Y”) instead of enforcing rules in GlideRecord scripts and Flow conditions.

title: Building on ServiceNow’s Latest AI: Practical Patterns for Now Assist, AI Control Tower, and Virtual Agent
excerpt: Learn how to apply the latest ServiceNow AI capabilities—including Now Assist v2.0 models, AI Control Tower, Virtual Agent AI, and AI Search—in real workflows. This guide focuses on concrete GlideRecord and Flow Designer patterns you can reuse in your own apps.
content:
Overview

ServiceNow’s AI stack has matured into a cohesive platform: updated Now Assist models, AI Control Tower, Predictive Intelligence, Virtual Agent AI, AI Search, and deep LLM integrations. Recent releases add higher-quality ServiceNow AI Models v2.0 for Now Assist, expanded Microsoft and third-party LLM integrations with governance, and new AI-powered experiences in workspace UIs.

For developers, the opportunity is to orchestrate these capabilities from server-side scripts and Flow Designer, so AI is embedded directly into records, tasks, and custom apps—not tacked on as a chatbot.

Implementation

Now Assist and ServiceNow AI Models v2.0

New instances and upgrades now default to ServiceNow AI Models v2.0 for Now Assist, improving summarization, action suggestions, and knowledge answers across workspaces.

A common pattern is to let Now Assist summarize large incident histories and save a concise summary on the record for reporting or handoffs.

// Example: Generate and persist an AI summary for an Incident
// Assumes you’ve configured Now Assist for ITSM and enabled summarization

var incidentGr = new GlideRecord('incident');
if (incidentGr.get(current.sys_id)) {
  // Build the prompt from comments/work notes
  var workNotes = '';
  var journalGr = new GlideRecord('sys_journal_field');
  journalGr.addQuery('element_id', current.sys_id);
  journalGr.addQuery('element', 'work_notes');
  journalGr.orderBy('sys_created_on');
  journalGr.query();
  while (journalGr.next()) {
    workNotes += '\n[' + journalGr.sys_created_on + '] ' + journalGr.value;
  }

  // Call a Scripted REST API or Script Include that wraps the GenAI Controller / Now Assist APIs
  var ai = new NowAssistUtils(); // your Script Include
  var summary = ai.summarizeIncident(incidentGr.number.toString(), workNotes);

  incidentGr.u_ai_summary = summary;
  incidentGr.update();
}

In this pattern, the Script Include encapsulates Now Assist / GenAI Controller calls, keeping your business logic clean.

AI Control Tower, Predictive Intelligence, and Flow Designer

AI Control Tower centralizes LLMs (ServiceNow models plus Microsoft/OpenAI/etc.), safety rules, and usage policies. Predictive Intelligence continues to drive auto-routing, categorization, and recommendations based on ML models trained on your data.

A typical developer workflow:

  1. Use Predictive Intelligence to auto-classify and route records.
  2. Use AI Control Tower to call a governed LLM for generative tasks (summaries, drafts, explanations).
  3. Orchestrate both via Flow Designer actions and subflows.
// Server-side helper: invoke an AI Control Tower endpoint via REST

var AiTowerClient = Class.create();
AiTowerClient.prototype = {
  initialize: function() {},

  generateResolutionSuggestion: function(incidentSysId) {
    var inc = new GlideRecord('incident');
    if (!inc.get(incidentSysId))
      return '';

    var r = new sn_ws.RESTMessageV2('x_your_app.ai_control_tower', 'generate_resolution');
    r.setRequestBody(JSON.stringify({
      short_description: inc.short_description.toString(),
      description: inc.description.toString(),
      category: inc.category.toString(),
      subcategory: inc.subcategory.toString()
    }));

    var res = r.execute();
    var body = res.getBody();
    var parsed = JSON.parse(body);
    return parsed.suggestion || '';
  },

  type: 'AiTowerClient'
};

In Flow Designer, expose this via an Action that takes an Incident Sys ID and writes the returned suggestion to a work note or custom field.

Virtual Agent AI, NLU, and MCP / Agent-to-Agent

Virtual Agent now uses generative AI to handle more open-ended questions, with improved NLU models. With Agent-to-Agent (A2A) and MCP-style protocols, you can let ServiceNow agents collaborate with external AI agents or tools while keeping the Virtual Agent conversation in control.

Typical integration pattern:

  • Virtual Agent topic collects user intent and context.
  • Flow Designer subflow calls an external tool or AI agent (via API, MCP, or other protocol).
  • Virtual Agent presents the AI agent’s result, with guardrails defined in AI Control Tower.
// Example: GlideRecord step in a Virtual Agent action to fetch user’s open requests

var gr = new GlideRecord('sc_request');
gr.addQuery('requested_for', gs.getUserID());
gr.addActiveQuery();
gr.orderByDesc('sys_created_on');
gr.setLimit(5);
gr.query();

var results = [];
while (gr.next()) {
  results.push({
    number: gr.number.toString(),
    short_description: gr.short_description.toString(),
    state: gr.state.getDisplayValue()
  });
}

// Pass 'results' back to Virtual Agent as an array to render in a carousel or list

LLM Integration Patterns and AI Search

ServiceNow now supports seamless integration with Microsoft AI services and other LLMs, coordinated through AI Control Tower. AI Search provides vector-based, relevance-tuned search across records and knowledge.

Common patterns:

  • AI Search widget/Global Search with AI-powered answer snippets.
  • Server-side retrieve-then-generate: query AI Search, then send top results to an LLM via AI Control Tower for a tailored answer.
// Pseudo-pattern: retrieve-then-generate using AI Search + LLM

var query = 'How do I reset my VPN token?';

// 1. AI Search (example, using a custom Scripted REST or API wrapper)
var aiSearch = new AiSearchUtils();
var docs = aiSearch.searchKnowledge(query, 5); // returns array of {number, short_description, text}

// 2. Compose context for LLM
var contextText = '';
docs.forEach(function(doc, idx) {
  contextText += '\n[' + (idx+1) + '] ' + doc.short_description + '\n' + doc.text + '\n';
});

// 3. Call AI Control Tower to generate a consolidated answer
var tower = new AiTowerClient();
var answer = tower.generateAnswerFromContext(query, contextText);

// 4. Persist or return the answer
current.u_ai_answer = answer;
current.update();

Best Practices

  • Centralize AI calls in Script Includes: Wrap Now Assist, AI Control Tower, and external LLM calls in Script Includes to keep flows, UI Actions, and Business Rules simple.
  • Use Flow Designer for orchestration: Trigger AI-processing subflows from lifecycle events (create/update/close) instead of one-off scripts in forms.
  • Start with narrow, high-value use cases: Summaries, resolution suggestions, and classification are safer first steps than full autonomous flows.
  • Leverage AI Control Tower policies: Define which tables, fields, and roles are allowed to send data to external LLMs; log and review usage.
  • Keep prompts and context minimal but rich: Provide only relevant fields and a small set of related records or knowledge articles to reduce hallucination and latency.
  • Design Virtual Agent topics with clear guardrails: Use intent detection and topic routing; fall back to classic scripted paths when confidence is low.
  • Monitor and retrain Predictive Intelligence models: Regularly review classification accuracy and retrain when data or routing logic changes.
  • Version your prompts: Store prompts and config in sys_properties or custom tables so you can iterate without code changes.

Common Pitfalls

  • Calling LLMs directly from many places: Scattering REST calls in Business Rules, Scripted REST APIs, and UI Actions leads to inconsistent behavior and policy bypass. Always route through a shared utility or AI Control Tower configuration.
  • Sending full records or logs to external models: Dumping entire incident histories or knowledge bases risks PII/PHI exposure and bloats tokens. Always filter to the minimal needed fields and anonymize where possible.
  • Skipping data hygiene before Predictive Intelligence: Training models on dirty or inconsistent data yields poor routing and recommendations. Clean your categories, assignment groups, and mandatory fields first.
  • Over-automating Virtual Agent: Letting generative responses handle every query without explicit intents, disambiguation, or exit paths frustrates users. Preserve deterministic flows for critical processes.
  • Ignoring observability: Not logging prompts, responses, and decisions from AI-powered flows makes debugging and compliance audits difficult. Capture AI activity (with redaction) in a dedicated log table or ATF tests.
  • Blocking human override: AI-suggested categories, resolutions, or summaries must be editable by agents. Avoid hard enforcement via Business Rules that reject human corrections.
  • Tight coupling to a single LLM provider: Hard-coding vendor-specific APIs undermines AI Control Tower’s value. Use its abstraction so you can switch providers without rewriting flows.

title: This Week’s ServiceNow Platform Updates: Yokohama/Xanadu, Impact Platform Health, and Employee Center
excerpt: This guide distills the latest ServiceNow platform updates from official docs and community posts into concrete actions for developers. Learn what’s new in Yokohama/Xanadu, Impact Platform Health, Employee Center, and how to safely upgrade, harden security, and improve performance with practical examples.
content:
Overview

The past week has brought a cluster of important ServiceNow updates across the core platform, Impact Platform Health, Employee Center, and Store apps. As a developer, these changes affect how you plan Yokohama/Xanadu upgrades, monitor platform health, and deliver better employee experiences.

This guide focuses on what you can act on now: how to prepare and test upgrades, wire the new Platform Health capabilities into your workflows, adopt Employee Center enhancements, and apply security and performance best practices from recent knowledge content.

Yokohama/Xanadu Release Features and Upgrade Guidance

ServiceNow continues to ship patches and hotfixes for the Yokohama family, with updated guidance in the official release notes and upgrade center.

Key themes for Yokohama/Xanadu

  • Ongoing patches and hotfixes – The Yokohama release notes list new patch levels and important fixes across platform, security, and performance.
  • App Version–aware upgrades – Recent Platform Academy content highlights strategies to upgrade with confidence using app versioning and consistent automation.
  • AI-first capabilities – The core platform continues to evolve as an AI control tower, so instances should be kept close to current families to leverage these capabilities.

Practical upgrade flow

  1. Inventory and freeze

    Identify in-progress development and freeze non-critical changes before requesting an upgrade in your sub‑prod instances.

    // Simple inventory of in-progress update sets
var us = new GlideRecord('sys_update_set');
us.addActiveQuery();
us.addQuery('state', 'in progress');
us.query();
while (us.next()) {
  gs.print(us.name + ' - ' + us.sys_id);
}
  2. Align app versions

    Use the application manager to confirm your scoped apps are on versions compatible with Yokohama/Xanadu before scheduling the family upgrade.

  3. Automate regression checks

    Register critical-path checks in ATF (Automated Test Framework) and run them as a gate before and after upgrading each environment.

    // Example: create an ATF test programmatically
var test = new GlideRecord('sys_atf_test');
test.initialize();
test.name = 'Critical Incident Flow – Post-Upgrade';
test.description = 'Validates core incident creation and assignment.';
test.active = true;
var testId = test.insert();
// Add steps via ATF APIs or UI as needed
  4. Promote with app version control

    Use a consistent promotion pattern (dev → test → prod) and avoid local hotfixes that diverge app versions by environment.

Anti‑patterns to avoid

  • Upgrading production before running ATF and sanity checks on a representative sub‑prod environment.
  • Skipping app version review and discovering incompatibilities only after the family upgrade.
  • Leaving long‑lived in‑progress update sets that span multiple family versions.

Platform Health and Impact Capabilities Updates

The December Store release introduces expanded ServiceNow Impact Platform Health capabilities, including real-time prevention, diagnostic scans, and improved dashboards for developers.

What’s new in Impact Platform Health

  • Real-Time Messaging & Prevention – Proactive alerts and preventive guidance when risky configurations or patterns are detected in near real time.
  • Automated Diagnostic Scans – Configurable scans that run nightly, weekly, or monthly to detect common issues across your instance landscape.
  • Developer-centric Dashboards – Each developer gets a personalized view of findings, exceptions, and technical debt to prioritize remediation.

Configuring scheduled diagnostic scans

Platform Health configuration lets admins define scan cadences per instance. You can also trigger scans or respond to findings with server-side logic.

// Example: post-scan handler to create tasks for high severity findings
var finding = new GlideRecord('sn_impact_ph_finding');
finding.addQuery('severity', 'high');
finding.addQuery('state', 'new');
finding.query();
while (finding.next()) {
  var task = new GlideRecord('sn_custom_tech_debt');
  task.initialize();
  task.short_description = 'Platform Health finding: ' + finding.name;
  task.description = finding.description;
  task.priority = 1; // Critical
  task.u_finding = finding.sys_id;
  task.insert();

  finding.state = 'task_created';
  finding.update();
}

Best practices for Platform Health adoption

  • Start with weekly scans in non‑prod to tune noise, then enable nightly scans in production.
  • Treat findings as work items: route to the right teams, track SLAs, and close the loop with root-cause fixes.
  • Use developer dashboards in sprint planning to prioritize high-impact debt over low‑value cosmetic fixes.

Common Platform Health anti‑patterns

  • Running scans but not integrating findings into any work intake process (they quickly become ignored noise).
  • Disabling rules that generate findings instead of remediating underlying issues.
  • Scanning only production while ignoring technical debt accumulating in dev/test.

Store App Releases and Employee Center Enhancements

The December 2025 Store release also delivers new features across ServiceNow Impact and Employee Center (Pro).

Employee Center (Pro) December enhancements

Recent enhancements focus on improving discoverability, content targeting, and experience configuration.

  • Richer Employee Center layouts – New layout options and page components make it easier to compose branded, task-focused employee hubs.
  • Improved content targeting – Finer-grained criteria for who sees which content, driven by user attributes and contextual signals.
  • Better search and topic experience – Updated search components and topic pages to surface relevant knowledge and services more quickly.

Practical configuration example

// Example: Assign a topic page to a specific user criteria
var crit = new GlideRecord('sn_ec_user_criteria');
crit.addQuery('name', 'Canada Employees');
crit.query();
if (crit.next()) {
  var topic = new GlideRecord('sn_ec_topic_page');
  topic.addQuery('title', 'Benefits & Leave');
  topic.query();
  if (topic.next()) {
    var map = new GlideRecord('sn_ec_topic_user_criteria_m2m');
    map.initialize();
    map.topic_page = topic.sys_id;
    map.user_criteria = crit.sys_id;
    map.insert();
  }
}

Impact Store updates you should care about

  • New Platform Health experiences – The December Impact Store release bundles the Platform Health improvements described above.
  • Store delivery model – Many Impact capabilities are delivered via the Store, so staying current with Store app versions is as important as family upgrades.

Security Patches and Performance Improvements

The Yokohama release notes and available patches pages highlight ongoing security and performance fixes for the family.

Actionable security steps

  • Track the latest Yokohama patches and apply them to non-prod quickly, promoting to prod after validation.
  • Enable and monitor security-related system properties recommended by release notes (for example, stricter default ACL behavior or encryption options where available).
  • Use Impact Platform Health to surface insecure patterns, such as global ACLs or direct table writes from client scripts.
// Example: quick scan for overly permissive ACLs
var acl = new GlideRecord('sys_security_acl');
acl.addQuery('type', 'record');
acl.addNullQuery('condition');
acl.addNullQuery('script');
acl.query();
while (acl.next()) {
  gs.print('ACL without condition/script: ' + acl.name + ' on ' + acl.operation);
}

Performance tuning themes

  • Apply hotfixes aimed at query performance and caching issues listed in the Yokohama patches page.
  • Use Performance Analytics, Platform Health, and logs to find slow transactions and long-running scripts.
  • Refactor synchronous work into background or asynchronous flows where latency is not user‑critical.

Best Practices from Recent Knowledge and Community Content

Recent Knowledge Base and community posts emphasize predictable upgrades, AI‑ready architectures, and disciplined configuration practices.

Key best practices

  • Design for AI-first features – Use standard data models, consistent task types, and well-defined APIs so generative and agentic AI features can reason over your workflows.
  • Favor configuration over customization – Use out-of-the-box flows, UI components, and patterns first; only customize where there is clear, quantified value.
  • Treat Store app versions as first-class – Establish a cadence to review and update Store apps (Impact, Employee Center, etc.) alongside family upgrades.
  • Automate guardrails – Capture guardrails (naming, ACL rules, integration patterns) as code and checks, not tribal knowledge.
// Guardrail example: prevent creation of client scripts on core tables via business rule
if (current.table == 'incident') {
  gs.addErrorMessage('Client scripts on incident are restricted. Use UI Policies or UX Components.');
  current.setAbortAction(true);
}

Common anti‑patterns highlighted in knowledge content

  • Running upgrades and Store app updates without documented rollback and test plans.
  • Using Employee Center as a static portal instead of an actively curated, data-driven experience.
  • Ignoring Impact Platform Health findings because "prod is working" until a critical incident occurs.

New Features in ServiceNow Impact Platform Health

Developers can also use server-side scripts to quickly triage and remediate findings identified by Platform Health scans. For example, the following GlideRecord script locates open technical debt findings assigned to the current user and updates their status after remediation:

var grFinding = new GlideRecord('imp_ph_finding'); // Example Platform Health finding table
grFinding.addActiveQuery();
grFinding.addQuery('assigned_to', gs.getUserID());
grFinding.addQuery('priority', '<=', 3); // Focus on higher-priority issues
grFinding.query();

while (grFinding.next()) {
    // Add custom logic here to verify the finding was remediated
    if (/* remediation check passes */ true) {
        grFinding.state = 'resolved';
        grFinding.resolution_notes = 'Resolved as part of December 2025 technical debt cleanup.';
        grFinding.update();
    }
}

To operationalize Platform Health, many teams schedule background jobs to create work items (such as Stories or Tasks) for critical findings. The following example shows how you might automatically create Agile stories from high-impact findings to ensure they are tracked in sprint planning:

var finding = new GlideRecord('imp_ph_finding');
finding.addActiveQuery();
finding.addQuery('impact_score', '>=', 80); // Example impact threshold
finding.addQuery('story_created', false);
finding.query();

while (finding.next()) {
    var story = new GlideRecord('rm_story');
    story.initialize();
    story.short_description = 'Remediate Platform Health finding ' + finding.number;
    story.description = 'Finding: ' + finding.short_description + '\nRule: ' + finding.rule_name +

    story.assignment_group = finding.assignment_group;
    var storySysId = story.insert();

    finding.story_created = true;
    finding.story = storySysId;
    finding.update();
}

content:
Overview — What's Changed and Why It Matters

ServiceNow integration patterns continue to converge on three goals: make integrations more resilient at scale, reduce custom code, and enable real-time or near-real-time data flows via streaming where appropriate.

Updated Integration Patterns to Use

  • API-first flow (REST/Scripted REST) for synchronous interactions: Use when a synchronous response is required. For example, create a Scripted REST API to handle synchronous updates from external systems. Here's a practical example of a Scripted REST resource that processes incoming incident data:
    • var IncidentAPI = Class.create();
IncidentAPI.prototype = Object.extendsObject(AbstractAjaxProcessor, {
    createIncident: function() {
        var short_desc = this.getParameter('sysparm_short_description');
        var caller_id = this.getParameter('sysparm_caller_id');
        
        var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
        gr.initialize();
        gr.short_description = short_desc;
        gr.caller_id = caller_id;
        var sys_id = gr.insert();
        
        return 'Incident created with sys_id: ' + sys_id;
    },
    
    type: 'IncidentAPI'
});
  • Event/Stream-based for high-volume or low-latency needs: Use Stream Connect or message producers for telemetry. Publish events using GlideEventManager for real-time notifications in high-volume scenarios.
  • ETL/Batch for bulk data and CMDB population: Use Integration Hub ETL actions for large imports. A GlideRecord example for bulk CMDB updates might look like this, ensuring efficient querying and updates:
    • var ciGr = new GlideRecord('cmdb_ci_server');
ciGr.addQuery('name', 'IN', bulkNames.join(','));
ciGr.query();
while (ciGr.next()) {
    ciGr.u_last_scan_date = new GlideDateTime();
    ciGr.u_scan_status = 'Complete';
    ciGr.update();
}
  • Process API + Orchestration for cross-system workflows: Create lightweight process APIs that encapsulate business rules.

Practical Flow Designer Tips

  • Prefer subflows and reusable flow actions: Encapsulate repeated logic into subflows or custom actions. In a custom Script Step within Flow Designer, you can use GlideRecord for reusable data operations, such as updating a related record:
    • (function execute(inputs, outputs) {
    var triggerRecord = inputs.trigger_record; // Data pill from trigger
    
    var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
    if (gr.get(triggerRecord.sys_id)) {
        gr.state = 6; // Resolved
        gr.close_notes = 'Resolved via Flow Designer subflow';
        gr.update();
        outputs.resolved_incident = gr.getUniqueValue();
    }
})(inputs, outputs);
  • Implement defensive error handling: Add retry policies, exponential backoff, and compensating flows. Use Script Steps to log errors and trigger notifications.
  • Leverage dynamic inputs/outputs: Use introspection-capable actions to reduce maintenance. For dynamic REST calls in Flow Designer, reference data pills directly in REST Message actions.
  • Test with both unit and integration scenarios: Create mock REST endpoints and automate flow tests. Mock endpoints can simulate external APIs during testing.

Integration Hub Updates

  • Starter Package: Basic SOAP/REST steps, JDBC, PowerShell, SFTP/SSH. These provide out-of-the-box actions for common integrations without custom scripting.
  • Professional Package: Advanced features like introspection for dynamic data handling. Introspection allows Flow Designer actions to automatically map fields from external APIs, minimizing hardcoded configurations.

By adopting these patterns and tips, developers can build more scalable integrations while minimizing custom code maintenance. For instance, combining API-first flows with Flow Designer subflows enables orchestrated, resilient processes across systems. Always test flows thoroughly using the built-in execution details to verify data flow and error handling.

title: Mastering ServiceNow Integrations in 2025: New Patterns, Flow Designer Tips, and Integration Hub Updates
excerpt: Discover the latest ServiceNow integration patterns with the updated Decision Tree, essential Flow Designer tips for efficient automation, and key Integration Hub enhancements like 200+ new connectors.
content:
New ServiceNow Integration Patterns for 2025

ServiceNow's Integration Pattern Decision Tree, updated to version 3.1 in September 2025, provides a flowchart to select the optimal pattern for third-party connections.

  • Real-time pull: Use SubFlow with Integration Hub for synchronous responses via Scripted REST API.
  • Scheduled imports: Leverage Integration Hub ETL, Process API, or Table API for CMDB data.
  • High-volume streaming: Opt for Flow Action Kafka Producer step or Scriptable ProducerV2 API in Stream Connect.

For real-time pull patterns, expose a Scripted REST API to handle inbound webhook-style calls from external systems. This example demonstrates a basic Scripted REST API endpoint that processes incoming incident data, validates it, and creates a record using GlideRecord.

(function process(/*RESTAPIRequest*/ request, /*RESTAPIResponse*/ response) {
    var data = request.body.data;
    if (!data || !data.number || !data.short_description) {
        response.setStatus(400);
        response.setBody({error: 'Missing required fields'});
        return;
    }
    
    var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
    gr.initialize();
    gr.number = data.number;
    gr.short_description = data.short_description;
    gr.insert();
    
    response.setBody({sys_id: gr.sys_id.toString(), message: 'Incident created successfully'});
})(request, response);

This code validates the payload at the API boundary, rejects invalid data early, and uses GlideRecord for persistence, aligning with best practices for synchronous integrations.

Flow Designer Tips for Developers

Flow Designer simplifies no-code/low-code automation, especially with Integration Hub. Key tips include:

  • Combine REST/SOAP steps with Payload Builder, Retry Policies, and Remote Tables for robust flows.
  • Implement error handling in Data Stream actions with Stream Connect alerts from the Yokohama release.
  • For custom needs, build Integration Hub-compatible spokes or use professional packages.

When building flows for scheduled imports or high-volume data processing, use GlideRecord queries to handle CMDB data efficiently. Here's a practical example of a script step in Flow Designer that queries and transforms CMDB configuration items (CIs) before pushing to an external system via a REST step.

var gr = new GlideRecord('cmdb_ci');
gr.addQuery('install_status', '1'); // Active CIs only
gr.query();

var cis = [];
while (gr.next()) {
    cis.push({
        name: gr.name.toString(),
        sys_id: gr.sys_id.toString(),
        serial_number: gr.serial_number.toString()
    });
}

// Output to flow context for REST step
fd_data.output.cis = cis;

This script can be placed in a "Script" action within Flow Designer, filtering CIs by install status and preparing JSON output for downstream REST or ETL actions. Pair it with Retry Policies to ensure reliability during high-volume operations.

For custom spokes or advanced error handling, create a Scripted REST API that integrates with Table API logic. This example shows a GET endpoint for facilities data, which could be called from a Flow Designer REST step, demonstrating dynamic querying and response formatting.

(function process(request, response) {
    var facilities = [];
    var gr = new GlideRecord('cmdb_ci_server'); // Example table for servers as facilities
    if (request.queryParams.location) {
        gr.addQuery('location', request.queryParams.location);
    }
    gr.query();
    while (gr.next()) {
        facilities.push({
            id: gr.sys_id.toString(),
            name: gr.name.toString(),
            location: gr.location.toString()
        });
    }
    response.setBody({
        count: facilities.length,
        result: facilities
    });
})(request, response);

Use this pattern in Flow Designer by configuring a REST step to call your instance's endpoint, leveraging query parameters for conditional logic and ensuring schema consistency for reusable flows.

Integration Hub Updates and Expansion

Integration Hub now boasts over 200 pre-built connectors, enabling thousands of quick setups without custom code.

  • Starter Package: Basic SOAP/REST steps, JDBC, PowerShell, SFTP/SSH.
  • Professional Package: Advanced features like introspection for dynamic data handling.

With the Professional Package, leverage introspection in custom actions for dynamic inputs. The code examples above integrate seamlessly with spokes, allowing developers to extend pre-built connectors—for instance, by calling the CMDB GlideRecord script from a custom Kafka consumer flow or using the incident API in webhook-triggered subflows.

These patterns and code snippets empower developers to build scalable, maintainable integrations that scale with ServiceNow's 2025 advancements in Integration Hub and Flow Designer.

title: This Week in Enterprise AI: GenAI, LLMs, and Agents — Practical Takeaways for ServiceNow Developers
excerpt: Major vendors released model and agent updates this week that push multimodal reasoning, cheaper inference, and agent-first integrations. ServiceNow developers should focus on connectors, orchestration, security, and observability.
content:
Key Developments and What They Mean

This week saw coordinated advances from major AI vendors emphasizing multimodal LLMs, lower-cost inference, and agentic capabilities that are moving autonomous workflows from experiments into production.

  • Multimodal, higher-reasoning models are now mainstream — Vendors announced new multimodal releases with improved reasoning and coding skills, enabling agents to process text, images, and structured data seamlessly for richer ServiceNow integrations.
