  • Costs and performance improve — Recent launches include lower-priced model variants and faster inference tiers, making scalable AI adoption feasible for enterprise ServiceNow projects without prohibitive expenses.

Top Practical Actions for ServiceNow Projects

ServiceNow developers should prioritize connectors, orchestration, security, and observability to leverage these advancements effectively. Here's how to implement them with code examples and best practices.

  • Design agent interfaces, not just prompts — Define a clear agent contract: input context, allowed tools, retry/timeout policies. Use ServiceNow Flow Designer to orchestrate agent calls. 
    var inputs = {
  context: current.variables.user_query,
  tools: ['incident_lookup', 'update_record']
};
var agentResponse = sn_ws.RESTMessageV2.executeAction('ai_agent', inputs);
  • Build robust connectors and adapters — Prioritize lightweight, auditable adapters to target internal systems like Incident or CMDB tables. Use IntegrationHub for secure, reusable connectors. 
    var connector = new sn_Connect.ServiceNowConnector();
connector.setBasicAuth('token');
var response = connector.post('https://api.model-provider.com/v1/chat', payload);
    Focus on error handling and retry logic to ensure reliability.
  • Implement observability and tracing — Add request/response tracing and action logs to ServiceNow workflows. Leverage Performance Analytics and Security Incident Response for real-time monitoring. 
    gs.info('AI Agent Trace: Input=' + JSON.stringify(inputs) + ', Output=' + JSON.stringify(response));
new GlideRecord('sys_audit').insert({
  tablename: 'incident',
  sys_created_by: gs.getUserID(),
  fieldname: 'ai_agent_log'
});
    This enables anomaly detection and debugging in production.
  • Embed security and least-privilege in agents — Give agents scoped, tokenized credentials and enforce RBAC policies. Follow ServiceNow's shared responsibility model by implementing Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) and Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) for all integrations.

Security Best Practices for AI Agents in ServiceNow

Security is critical as agents gain autonomy and access sensitive data. Adopt these practices to design secure autonomy, monitor threats, and protect the full stack, drawing from ServiceNow's 2025 guidelines.

  • Implement RBAC for agents — Define agent roles with least-privilege access, limiting data and actions to essentials. Use ServiceNow roles like ai_agent_executor with scoped ACLs. 
    // Example ACL script for agent access
answer = gs.getUser().hasRole('ai_agent_executor') && 
         current.sys_id == gs.getUser().getRecord().sys_id;
    Routine reviews prevent over-permissioning.
  • Enable MFA and adaptive authentication — Require MFA for high-risk users and agents initiating actions. Configure step-up authentication based on context like IP or risk score. 
    // In Flow Designer, add MFA check
if (!user.hasMFA()) {
  gs.eventQueue('mfa.required', current, gs.getUserID(), '');
}
  • Enforce encryption and secure integrations — Use TLS for data in transit, Edge Encryption for data at rest, and anonymize PII before agent processing. Secure APIs with token-based auth. 
    var rest = new sn_ws.RESTMessageV2();
rest.setRequestHeader('Authorization', 'Bearer ' + scopedToken);
rest.setRequestHeader('Content-Type', 'application/json');
  • Real-time monitoring and threat detection — Use Security Operations for AI-driven anomaly detection. Log all agent actions and enable sandboxing to contain compromised agents. 
    // Log for observability
var log = new GlideRecord('syslog_ai_agent');
log.initialize();
log.message = 'Agent action: ' + action;
log.insert();
  • Regular audits and patching — Schedule security audits via Security Center, apply patches promptly, and test updates in sub-prod. Avoid common pitfalls like weak passwords or ignoring logs.

ServiceNow's AI Platform emphasizes confidential compute and LLM routers with consistent security protocols, ensuring agents scale securely.

Orchestration Patterns and Architectures to Adopt

  • Hybrid orchestration layer — Place an orchestration service between ServiceNow and model endpoints using Scripted REST APIs or Flow Designer. This centralizes connectors, security, and observability. 
    // Orchestrator example
function orchestrateAgent(inputs) {
  var securityCheck = validateRBAC(inputs);
  if (!securityCheck) throw 'Access denied';
  var response = callModel(inputs);
  logTrace(response);
  return response;
}
  • Agent capability registry — Maintain a registry of available agent tools with metadata in a custom table like ai_agent_tools. Query it dynamically for tool selection. 
    var tools = new GlideRecord('ai_agent_tools');
tools.addQuery('active', true);
tools.query();
while (tools.next()) {
  agentTools.push(tools.getValue('tool_name'));
}
  • Human-in-the-loop checkpoints — Design approval steps for high-impact actions using Approval activities in Flow Designer. Combine with observability for audit trails.
  • Multi-agent collaboration — Use protocols like A2A for agent-to-agent communication, wrapped in authentication and sabotage detection.

Getting Started Checklist

  • Review your instance against ServiceNow Security Best Practices Guide (Zurich release).
  • Prototype a secure agent in a dev instance with RBAC and tracing.
  • Integrate observability dashboards for agent metrics.
  • Conduct a security audit focused on AI integrations.

By focusing on these areas, ServiceNow developers can build production-ready GenAI agents that are secure, observable, and scalable.

Actionable Best Practices

    // REST API example to trigger a scan (called from Flow Designer or IntegrationHub)
var request = new sn_ws.RESTMessageV2();
request.setEndpoint('https://yourinstance.service-now.com/api/now/table/sys_diagnostic_scan');
request.setHttpMethod('POST');

appGr.query();

    This helps identify app versions needing updates during upgrade planning, aligning with ServiceNow's app-version strategy.
  • Embed governance into pipelines: Enforce automated checks in CI/CD pipelines. For upgrade confidence, script checks against deprecated APIs or inefficient patterns flagged by HealthScan, using GlideRecord to scan business rules or scripts.
    var ruleGr = new GlideRecord('sys_script');
ruleGr.addQuery('script', 'CONTAINS', ' GlideRecord'); // Check for inefficient patterns
ruleGr.addQuery('inactive', false);
ruleGr.query();
while (ruleGr.next()) {
    if (ruleGr.script.indexOf('query()') !== -1) { // Simplified deprecated check
        gs.warn('Potential inefficient query in: ' + ruleGr.name);
    }
}
    This governance script can run in pipelines to preempt HealthScan findings, reducing technical debt proactively.

By incorporating these code examples into your development practices, you can operationalize Platform Health features, automate remediation workflows, and ensure smoother upgrades across your ServiceNow instances.

Introduction to 2025 Enterprise Trends

Enterprise automation in 2025 is dominated by hyperautomation, AI-driven processes, and low-code platforms, fundamentally reshaping ITSM and digital transformation. These trends enable end-to-end automation of business processes, reducing costs by up to 30% and enhancing scalability.

Hyperautomation: The Core of Enterprise Efficiency

Hyperautomation, coined by Gartner, combines RPA, AI, machine learning, and process mining to automate interconnected tasks across organizations. In ITSM, this means automating ticket resolution, service requests, and compliance checks seamlessly.

By 2025, hyperautomation optimizes finance, customer service, and logistics, with cloud trends like Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) and DevOps CI/CD pipelines accelerating deployments. ServiceNow's IT Operations Management (ITOM) module supports IaC for Visibility and Service Mapping.

AI and ML: Intelligent ITSM Workflows

AI integration is central, with NLP platforms automating customer interactions and ML for anomaly detection. In ServiceNow, Virtual Agent and Predictive Intelligence use ML to forecast incidents and auto-resolve issues.

Low-Code/No-Code: Democratizing Automation

No-code platforms empower non-developers, but ServiceNow's App Engine and Creator Workflows take this further for enterprise ITSM. Build custom apps without deep coding, automating approvals and change management.

ITSM-Specific Impacts and ServiceNow Strategies

  • Implement hyperautomation: Use Orchestration and RPA Hub to chain workflows.
  • AI for predictions: Train models in Studio for incident prioritization.
  • Low-code ITSM apps: Rapidly prototype with Studio, deploy via Store.
  • Security focus: Automate vulnerability response with SecOps.

title: December 2025: Key ServiceNow Platform Updates, Features, and Best Practices for Developers
excerpt: This week's ServiceNow updates focus on platform health, agentic AI tooling, Employee Center enhancements, and Canadian public-sector AI investments — plus practical best practices for developers.
content:
Overview — What Changed This Week

ServiceNow's December 2025 wave emphasizes proactive platform health tooling, expanded agentic AI capabilities and protocols, targeted Employee Center improvements, and strategic investments to enable AI adoption in regulated environments.

New and Updated Platform Features

Platform Health (Impact): ServiceNow announced a new Platform Health capability in the Impact portfolio that provides scheduled diagnostic scans, real-time messaging for prevention, scan findings, and role-specific dashboards for executives and developers.

Agentic AI & A2A protocol support: The platform now recommends and supports A2A protocol v0.3 for agent-to-agent communications and documents OAuth 2.0 as the security scheme for those A2A flows.

Employee Center Pro — December enhancements: Employee Center received a December 2025 update with multiple UX and admin improvements.

Regional AI investments: ServiceNow announced a CA$110M multi-year investment to build Canada-hosted, AI-ready infrastructure.

Practical Best Practices for ServiceNow Developers

  • Adopt Platform Health scans early: Enable scheduled scans and route findings to developer dashboards.
  • Design for agentic workflows with security in mind: Follow the A2A v0.3 guidance and use OAuth2 for auth between agents.
  • Use app versioning to simplify upgrades: Maintain explicit app versions and test versioned apps in lower environments.
  • Instrument governance and policy-as-code: Embed guardrails in CI/CD for flows and agents.

Example: Query and route Platform Health findings to a developer dashboard

The following server-side script (for example in a Script Include or Scheduled Script Execution) demonstrates how you might query Platform Health scan findings and populate a simple custom table used to back a developer dashboard.

var findingGr = new GlideRecord('x_impact_ph_finding'); // example table for Platform Health findings
findingGr.addQuery('state', 'open');
findingGr.orderByDesc('risk_score');
findingGr.setLimit(100);
findingGr.query();

var devFindingGr = new GlideRecord('x_custom_dev_finding'); // your custom dashboard table
while (findingGr.next()) {
    devFindingGr.initialize();
    devFindingGr.u_finding = findingGr.getUniqueValue();
    devFindingGr.u_short_description = findingGr.getValue('short_description');
    devFindingGr.u_risk_score = findingGr.getValue('risk_score');
    devFindingGr.u_assigned_developer = findingGr.getValue('assigned_to');
    devFindingGr.u_scan_run = findingGr.getValue('scan_run');
    devFindingGr.insert();
}

Example: Flow Designer policy-as-code check for AI agent changes

You can use Flow Designer with custom actions to enforce guardrails when AI agent-related records are created or updated. The following pseudo-code shows a Script step in a Flow Designer action that validates changes to an AI agent configuration record before allowing the flow to proceed.

// This script runs in a Flow Designer "Run script" step
(function execute(inputs, outputs) {
    var agentGr = new GlideRecord('x_ai_agent_config');
    if (!agentGr.get(inputs.agent_sys_id)) {
        outputs.approved = false;
        outputs.message = 'Agent configuration not found.';
        return;
    }

    // Basic guardrail: prevent unapproved scopes in production
    var isProd = gs.getProperty('instance_type') === 'production';
    var requestedScope = agentGr.getValue('scope');

    if (isProd && requestedScope === 'global_unrestricted') {
        outputs.approved = false;
        outputs.message = 'Unrestricted global scope is not allowed in production.';
        return;
    }

    // Enforce maximum model temperature for regulated environments
    var temperature = parseFloat(agentGr.getValue('model_temperature')) || 0.0;
    if (temperature > 0.5) {
        outputs.approved = false;
        outputs.message = 'Model temperature exceeds approved threshold (0.5).';
        return;
    }

    outputs.approved = true;
    outputs.message = 'Agent change approved by policy-as-code.';
})(inputs, outputs);

Example: Calling a ServiceNow API with OAuth 2.0 from another agent

The following example uses a Scripted REST API or integration script in ServiceNow to act as an OAuth 2.0 client when communicating with another ServiceNow instance or external agent endpoint as part of an A2A v0.3 flow. It retrieves an access token from an OAuth profile and calls a remote agent API.

var client = new sn_ws.RESTMessageV2();
client.setHttpMethod('post');
client.setEndpoint('https://partner-instance.example.com/api/x_a2a/agent/v0_3/execute');

// Use an existing OAuth 2.0 profile configured in the instance
client.setAuthenticationProfile('oauth2', 'partner_oauth_profile');

// Set headers and payload expected by the A2A v0.3-compatible endpoint
client.setRequestHeader('Content-Type', 'application/json');
client.setRequestHeader('Accept', 'application/json');

var payload = {
    "agent_id": "routing_agent_01",
    "correlation_id": gs.generateGUID(),
    "task": {
        "type": "incident_resolution",
        "input": {
            "incident_number": "INC0010001"
        }
    },
    "context": {
        "source_instance": gs.getProperty('instance_name'),
        "requested_by": gs.getUserName()
    }
};

client.setRequestBody(JSON.stringify(payload));

var response = client.execute();
var status = response.getStatusCode();
var body = response.getBody();
gs.info('A2A call status: ' + status + ', response: ' + body);

Developer Checklist for the Next 30 Days

  • Enable Platform Health scans in a sandbox and review the first set of findings.
  • Assess any agentic workflows for compatibility with A2A v0.3.
  • Register apps with app versioning and review Platform Academy materials.
  • Update CI/CD to include policy-as-code checks for new AI agents.

By combining these new platform capabilities with practical automation patterns in scripts, flows, and integrations, ServiceNow developers can proactively manage technical debt, secure agentic workflows, and streamline adoption of December 2025 features across their environments.

title: Building AI Agents in ServiceNow: A Complete Guide
excerpt: Learn how to create intelligent AI agents that automate complex workflows using ServiceNow's AI capabilities and GenAI integration.
content:
Introduction

AI Agents are revolutionizing how enterprises handle automation. Unlike traditional workflows that follow rigid paths, AI agents can reason about context, make decisions, and take autonomous actions to achieve goals. In ServiceNow, these agents leverage Now Assist, Predictive Intelligence, and GenAI integrations to handle everything from incident resolution to complex approval workflows.

What are AI Agents?

AI Agents are autonomous systems that can perceive their environment, make decisions, and take actions to achieve specific goals. They differ from simple automation in three key ways:

  • Reasoning: Agents analyze context and determine the best course of action rather than following predetermined paths.
  • Tool usage: Agents can invoke APIs, query databases, and trigger workflows as needed.
  • Goal-oriented: Agents work toward outcomes rather than executing fixed sequences.

In ServiceNow, AI agents combine Virtual Agent conversations, Now Assist capabilities, and Flow Designer orchestration into cohesive autonomous systems.

Prerequisites

To build AI Agents in ServiceNow, you'll need:

  • ServiceNow Yokohama or later (Zurich recommended for full AI Control Tower)
  • AI Control Tower access and configuration
  • Integration Hub subscription for external tool connections
  • Now Assist entitlement for GenAI capabilities
  • Predictive Intelligence for ML-based routing and classification

Architecture Overview

A ServiceNow AI Agent consists of these components:

  • Agent Definition: Configuration that defines the agent's purpose, capabilities, and constraints.
  • Tool Registry: Available actions the agent can invoke (GlideRecord operations, REST calls, Flow triggers).
  • Context Manager: Gathers relevant data for decision-making (record history, user context, related CIs).
  • Orchestration Layer: Flow Designer flows that coordinate agent actions and handle outcomes.
  • Guardrails: Policies that constrain agent behavior and require human approval for high-risk actions.

Step 1: Configure AI Control Tower

AI Control Tower centralizes governance for all AI capabilities. Start by configuring policies for your agent.

// Check AI Control Tower readiness
var aiConfig = new GlideRecord('sn_ai_core_ai_config');
aiConfig.addQuery('active', true);
aiConfig.query();
if (aiConfig.next()) {
  gs.info('AI Control Tower active: ' + aiConfig.name);
  gs.info('Default model: ' + aiConfig.default_model);
} else {
  gs.warn('AI Control Tower not configured');
}

Configure these key settings in AI Control Tower:

  • Model selection: Choose which LLM handles which tasks (summarization, classification, generation).
  • Data policies: Define which fields and tables can be sent to AI models.
  • Logging: Enable prompt/response logging for audit and debugging.
  • Rate limits: Set usage thresholds to control costs and prevent abuse.

Step 2: Define Agent Capabilities

Create a Script Include that defines what your agent can do. Each capability maps to a specific action.

var IncidentResolutionAgent = Class.create();
IncidentResolutionAgent.prototype = {
  initialize: function(incidentSysId) {
    this.incidentGr = new GlideRecord('incident');
    this.incidentGr.get(incidentSysId);
    this.capabilities = [
      'summarize_history',
      'suggest_resolution',
      'find_similar_incidents',
      'auto_categorize',
      'notify_stakeholders'
    ];
  },

  // Capability: Summarize incident history
  summarizeHistory: function() {
    var notes = [];
    var journal = new GlideRecord('sys_journal_field');
    journal.addQuery('element_id', this.incidentGr.sys_id);
    journal.orderBy('sys_created_on');
    journal.setLimit(20);
    journal.query();
    while (journal.next()) {
      notes.push(journal.value.toString());
    }
    // Call Now Assist for summarization
    return this._callGenAI('summarize', notes.join('\n'));
  },

  // Capability: Find similar resolved incidents
  findSimilarIncidents: function() {
    var similar = [];
    var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
    gr.addQuery('state', 6); // Resolved
    gr.addQuery('category', this.incidentGr.category);
    gr.addQuery('sys_id', '!=', this.incidentGr.sys_id);
    gr.orderByDesc('sys_updated_on');
    gr.setLimit(5);
    gr.query();
    while (gr.next()) {
      similar.push({
        number: gr.number.toString(),
        resolution: gr.close_notes.toString(),
        short_description: gr.short_description.toString()
      });
    }
    return similar;
  },

  // Capability: Auto-categorize using Predictive Intelligence
  autoCategorize: function() {
    // Trigger PI classification
    var prediction = new global.PredictiveIntelligenceAPI();
    var result = prediction.getPrediction(
      'incident',
      this.incidentGr.sys_id,
      ['category', 'subcategory', 'assignment_group']
    );
    return result;
  },

  // Internal: Call GenAI via AI Control Tower
  _callGenAI: function(task, content) {
    try {
      var ai = new sn_ai.GenAIController();
      var response = ai.generate({
        task: task,
        content: content,
        max_tokens: 500
      });
      return response.text || '';
    } catch (e) {
      gs.error('GenAI call failed: ' + e.message);
      return '';
    }
  },

  type: 'IncidentResolutionAgent'
};

Step 3: Create Orchestration Flows

Use Flow Designer to orchestrate agent actions. The flow coordinates capabilities based on context and outcomes.

Agent Orchestration Flow Pattern:

  1. Trigger: Incident created or updated with specific conditions.
  2. Gather Context: Script step calls agent to collect relevant data.
  3. Analyze: Agent evaluates context and determines actions.
  4. Execute: Flow invokes appropriate capabilities based on agent decision.
  5. Validate: Check outcomes and determine if human review is needed.
  6. Complete: Update record with results and audit trail.
// Flow Designer Script Step: Agent Decision Logic
(function execute(inputs, outputs) {
  var agent = new IncidentResolutionAgent(inputs.incident_sys_id);
  
  // Step 1: Gather context
  var summary = agent.summarizeHistory();
  var similar = agent.findSimilarIncidents();
  var prediction = agent.autoCategorize();
  
  // Step 2: Determine confidence and action
  var confidence = parseFloat(prediction.confidence || 0);
  
  if (confidence >= 0.9 && similar.length > 0) {
    outputs.action = 'auto_resolve';
    outputs.suggested_resolution = similar[0].resolution;
    outputs.requires_approval = false;
  } else if (confidence >= 0.7) {
    outputs.action = 'suggest_resolution';
    outputs.suggested_resolution = similar.length > 0 ? similar[0].resolution : '';
    outputs.requires_approval = true;
  } else {
    outputs.action = 'escalate';
    outputs.suggested_resolution = '';
    outputs.requires_approval = true;
  }
  
  outputs.summary = summary;
  outputs.confidence = confidence;
})(inputs, outputs);

Step 4: Implement Guardrails

AI agents must have constraints to prevent unintended actions. Implement guardrails at multiple levels.

var AgentGuardrails = Class.create();
AgentGuardrails.prototype = {
  initialize: function() {
    this.highRiskActions = ['auto_resolve', 'reassign', 'close', 'delete'];
    this.confidenceThreshold = 0.85;
    this.requireApprovalRoles = ['itil_admin', 'incident_manager'];
  },

  // Check if action requires human approval
  requiresApproval: function(action, confidence, record) {
    // High-risk actions always need approval below threshold
    if (this.highRiskActions.indexOf(action) >= 0) {
      if (confidence < this.confidenceThreshold) {
        return true;
      }
    }
    
    // Priority 1 incidents always need human review
    if (record.priority == 1) {
      return true;
    }
    
    // VIP callers need approval
    var caller = new GlideRecord('sys_user');
    if (caller.get(record.caller_id) && caller.vip == true) {
      return true;
    }
    
    return false;
  },

  // Log agent decision for audit
  logDecision: function(agentName, action, confidence, approved, details) {
    var log = new GlideRecord('u_ai_agent_audit');
    log.initialize();
    log.u_agent_name = agentName;
    log.u_action = action;
    log.u_confidence = confidence;
    log.u_approved = approved;
    log.u_details = JSON.stringify(details);
    log.u_timestamp = new GlideDateTime();
    log.insert();
  },

  type: 'AgentGuardrails'
};

Step 5: Handle Agent-to-Agent Communication

For complex scenarios, multiple agents may need to collaborate. Use the A2A protocol pattern.

// Agent-to-Agent message handler
var AgentMessaging = Class.create();
AgentMessaging.prototype = {
  initialize: function(agentId) {
    this.agentId = agentId;
  },

  // Send task to another agent
  delegateTask: function(targetAgent, task, context) {
    var message = {
      from: this.agentId,
      to: targetAgent,
      task: task,
      context: context,
      timestamp: new GlideDateTime().getNumericValue(),
      correlation_id: gs.generateGUID()
    };
    
    // Queue message for target agent
    var queue = new GlideRecord('u_agent_message_queue');
    queue.initialize();
    queue.u_message = JSON.stringify(message);
    queue.u_target_agent = targetAgent;
    queue.u_status = 'pending';
    queue.insert();
    
    return message.correlation_id;
  },

  // Process incoming messages
  processMessages: function() {
    var queue = new GlideRecord('u_agent_message_queue');
    queue.addQuery('u_target_agent', this.agentId);
    queue.addQuery('u_status', 'pending');
    queue.query();
    
    while (queue.next()) {
      var message = JSON.parse(queue.u_message);
      this._handleMessage(message);
      queue.u_status = 'processed';
      queue.update();
    }
  },

  type: 'AgentMessaging'
};

Best Practices

  • Start narrow: Begin with a single, well-defined use case before expanding agent capabilities.
  • Always log decisions: Create an audit table to track all agent actions, inputs, and outcomes.
  • Human-in-the-loop: Require approval for high-impact actions until confidence is proven.
  • Test with edge cases: Agents must handle missing data, ambiguous inputs, and error conditions gracefully.
  • Monitor continuously: Track accuracy, false positives, and user overrides to tune agent behavior.
  • Version capabilities: Store capability definitions in versioned records so you can roll back changes.
  • Scope credentials: Give agents minimum necessary permissions via dedicated service accounts.

Common Pitfalls

  • Over-automation: Letting agents take destructive actions without approval gates leads to incidents.
  • Ignoring context limits: Sending too much data to GenAI models causes token limits and latency issues.
  • No fallback path: Agents must gracefully degrade when AI services are unavailable.
  • Skipping audit: Without decision logs, you cannot debug issues or demonstrate compliance.
  • Tight coupling: Hardcoding model endpoints instead of using AI Control Tower breaks governance.
  • Ignoring user feedback: Not capturing when users override agent suggestions prevents learning.

Conclusion

Building AI agents in ServiceNow requires combining multiple platform capabilities: AI Control Tower for governance, Now Assist for GenAI, Predictive Intelligence for ML, and Flow Designer for orchestration. Start with well-defined capabilities, implement strong guardrails, and continuously monitor agent performance. With this foundation, you can progressively expand agent autonomy as confidence grows.
